beats.say: Last time, three requests arrived that no document can answer.
Where is this order? That lives in the orders database.
Is there milk in Kothrud? That's the inventory service.
And issue a credit. That's the payments system. And it's not a question. It's an action. Today, Ask FreshCart stops just reading, and starts doing.
Chapter five. From assistant, to agent.
First, the obvious shortcut.
Why not just give the model a connection to the database, and let it run queries? What could go wrong?
Everything. A model can get confused. It can be tricked by text it reads. And it can't be held accountable.
Think of a restaurant. The customer doesn't walk into the kitchen. They write an order on a slip. The waiter checks it. And the kitchen cooks.
That's tool calling. The model is the customer, writing slips. Your code is the waiter, and the kitchen.
So what does the model see? A tool is one of your functions, described in plain words. A name, get order. And a description of what it does, and when to use it.
Plus a schema: the exact shape of its arguments. Here, one order id, as a string.
When the model wants a tool, its reply isn't text. It's a tool call: the name, the arguments, and an id.
And notice. The model has run nothing. Your code checks the call, runs it, and sends back the result, tagged with that same id.
This changes where safety lives. Only issue credits under two hundred rupees, written in the prompt, is a suggestion. The same check inside the function is a control.
The model's arguments are untrusted input. Validate them like data from a stranger: types, ranges, and whether this user may touch this order.
And errors are results too. If the orders service times out, send that back as the tool's result, so the model can adapt instead of crashing.
Meera asks for a smart assistant with twenty five tools, one for every FreshCart system.
Push back. Similar tools confuse the model's choice. Every tool's description costs tokens on every single request. And every tool can be misused.
Support needs about five. Get the order, search the policy, check stock, issue a credit behind an approval, and hand over to a human.
Next, answers that code can trust.
Ask a model for JSON, and sometimes you get: sure, here is the JSON. Or order id spelled differently. Your parser crashes.
So don't ask for a paragraph. Hand it a form. Fixed fields, fixed choices. The provider only lets the model produce output that fits. This is structured output.
One warning. The form can be filled perfectly, and still be wrong. Valid shape is not a correct answer.
Now, the big one.
FC two zero nine three one is late, and the milk was spoiled. What do I do? One tool call isn't enough. It needs the order. Then the policy. Then maybe a credit.
So put the tool call in a loop. The model thinks, asks for a tool, sees the result, and thinks again. Until it can answer. A model in a loop, choosing its next tool, is an agent.
Even this tiny loop needs a step limit, validation before running anything, errors returned as results, and every result tied to its call id.
You'll write that loop in every project.
And every time, you'll add the same things around it. Retries. A fallback model. Limits. Streaming. Traces. Approvals.
LangChain packages all of that. Its create agent function builds exactly the loop we just drew.
Then production arrives. One chat makes forty tool calls. A customer's email lands in a trace. The provider goes down on a Friday evening. Long chats get slow.

Middleware fixes these without rewriting the loop. Think of checkpoints on a conveyor belt. Every request passes a call limit, a data mask, a retry and fallback, and a summariser, on its way to the model.
Order matters. The first in the list wraps everything, so put logging and retries there. Put masking last, right before the model.
Last idea of the day.
Meera reads a week of chats. Some refund answers never searched the policy. The model decided it didn't need to. She wants rules. Can a loop where the model decides everything guarantee them?

It can't. When you need to decide the order of steps, you draw it yourself, like a subway map. Stations are steps. Lines are what runs next. And a switch sends the train back to rewrite when the results are weak. That's LangGraph.
Every station reads from a shared whiteboard, and writes only its own fields. That whiteboard is the state.
Now the policy search can't be skipped. There's simply no line around it.
LangGraph runs in rounds, called super steps.
In a round, every triggered step runs side by side. Searching the policy and fetching the order, together. Neither sees the other's update.
At the end of the round, the updates are merged, the state is saved, and the lines decide the next round.
Two parallel steps writing the same field, with no rule for merging, is an error. And a recursion limit caps the rounds, so nothing loops forever.
Let's lock it in.
Tool calling: the model writes the slip, your code cooks.
Structured output: hand it a form, not a blank page.
An agent is a model in a loop, choosing its next tool.
Middleware adds checkpoints, without rewriting the loop.
LangGraph lets you draw the map yourself.
And state is the whiteboard every step shares.
Ask FreshCart is a real agent now. Then production happens.
An agent asks about an order, steps away, and twenty minutes later types: and was the bread delivered? Ask FreshCart has no idea which order they mean.
The server crashes in the middle of an answer.
After one crash and an automatic retry, a customer is credited a hundred and fifty rupees. Twice.
And long chats get slower and pricier with every message. So where should a conversation live, so it survives a crash? And how do you make issue a credit safe to run twice?
That's chapter six. See you there.
